headline: Squid Balling Up in the Rips — Woods Hole and Quick's Hole Are Loading the Table
subhead: Bass and blues are eating well on the moving water while the bait build tells you what's coming behind it.
body_markdown:
I stood on the seawall at Woods Hole Monday evening watching squid stack up thick enough to turn the water gray under the dock lights, and that's the tell I wait for every July. Not albies yet — don't let anybody tell you different, it's too early, and anybody claiming false albacore in mid-July on this water is either lying or fishing somewhere else. But squid balling up like that in the current seams off the Steamship dock, sand eels flickering through Quick's Hole on the last of the ebb, mackerel schools ghosting through Robinson's Hole at first light — that's the bait signature that eventually turns into the run. Right now it's feeding stripers and blues, and that's plenty to keep me busy.

The better bass action this week has been on the outgoing tide at Robinson's Hole and Quick's Hole, working the current seams where the Elizabeth Islands squeeze the tide down into a fire hose. I've been running 1 to 1.5-ounce bucktails, white and chartreuse, bounced along bottom in 15 to 25 feet where the rip lays down current-side of the ledges. Fish are holding tight to structure — not chasing bait out into open water, making you come to them. Keeper-class stripers, 28 to 34 inches, with a few slot fish mixed in, came on that pattern Tuesday morning on the tail end of the ebb into the first hour of slack. Night tide has been better than day tide for the bigger fish — eels drifted through Quick's Hole after dark have out-produced the bucktail bite for size, though not for numbers. If you're set up to soak eels on a moving tide at Cuttyhunk's east end or the Robinson's Hole channel edge, that's where I'd put my night trip this week.

Bluefish have been the more reliable bite, and reliable is the word — not spectacular, but you can set your watch by it. Buzzards Bay side, off Wilbur's Point and running down toward the Cuttyhunk approach, blues have been blitzing on top most mornings before the wind builds. Choppers to 8 and 10 pounds are hammering topwater poppers and Ava 27 jigs worked fast through the froth. This bite window closes early — by mid-morning when the sun gets high and the surface goes glassy calm, the blues drop down and go quiet. Get out at first light or don't bother waiting around midday; I've wasted enough afternoons proving that to myself already this season.

Fluke fishing in Buzzards Bay has been a mixed bag, and I'll be straight about it — some drifts have been outstanding, others have been a grind for two or three keepers over three hours. The Quick's Hole channel and the sandy stretch off Cuttyhunk's north side have been the most consistent, drifting white and pink Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails in 20 to 35 feet on the incoming tide, when the current is pushing bait up out of the deeper holes onto the flats. Doormats haven't shown in numbers yet this year on my end of the water, but fish in the 18 to 22-inch range have been steady enough to make a dinner. If you're grinding it out and only picking at shorts, move — don't sit on dead water hoping it turns on. I've learned that lesson the hard way more times than I want to admit.

Scup fishing around the Woods Hole draw bridge and the rocky structure off Nonamesset has been the easy money this week — squid strips or sandworms on a simple sinker rig, and you can fill a cooler in an hour if you're patient about finding the right piece of structure on the drift. Good option for a slow-tide afternoon when the bass and blues have shut down and you still want to bend a rod.

As for what's coming — I keep one eye on Nantucket Sound and the Rhode Island side because that's where the squid concentrations are building fastest, and historically when that bait pushes hard into Vineyard Sound and the water settles into that comfortable summer warmth we associate with peak season, bonito start showing at Robinson's Hole before the albies ever do. That's usually a late-July into early-August event on my water, not a mid-July one, so I'm not chasing ghosts yet. What I am doing is fishing the rips hard on the moving tides, watching the bait every single trip, and keeping gear rigged for a quick switch — smaller profile Deadly Dicks and epoxy jigs staged and ready — because when that first bonito flash shows up in the froth off Menemsha, I want to be the first phone call at the dock, not the last one to hear about it. Until then, work the tide stages at Robinson's and Quick's Hole, fish the bluefish blitz early, and don't sleep on the scup if the bigger stuff goes quiet on you.
